title: SQLAlchemy and Alembic on PostgreSQL
summary: Map tables with SQLAlchemy 2 models, query them without N+1 problems, and change the schema safely with Alembic migrations.
intro: Most of an API's bugs and slow pages come from the database layer: a missing constraint, a query per row, a migration that loses data. Taskboard uses SQLAlchemy 2.1, written in the typed 2.0 style, with the psycopg 3 driver, PostgreSQL 18, and Alembic 1.20 for every schema change. In this lesson you read its models, the queries in its repositories, and its migrations, and pick up the habits that keep a schema and its code in step.

steps.title: Models with Mapped columns
steps.body:
A model is a Python class mapped to a table. In SQLAlchemy 2, each column is a class attribute typed with `Mapped[...]`, and the type decides a lot on its own:

- `Mapped[str]` is `NOT NULL`, and `Mapped[str | None]` allows `NULL`.
- `Mapped[date | None]` with no `mapped_column()` at all is a nullable `DATE`.
- `mapped_column()` adds the rest: a length, a foreign key, a default, an index.

Defaults come in two kinds. `default=` is filled in by Python when SQLAlchemy inserts the object. `server_default=` lives in the table itself, so rows that a migration or a script inserts get it too. Taskboard sets both where both matter.

Every model inherits one `Base`, whose `metadata` collects all the tables. Alembic compares that metadata with the database to write migrations, which is why `Base` also fixes how constraints are named.

examples.title: The Task model
examples.code:
class Task(TimestampMixin, Base):
    __tablename__ = "tasks"
    __table_args__ = (
        CheckConstraint("priority BETWEEN 1 AND 3", name="priority_range"),
        Index("ix_tasks_project_id_status_position", "project_id", "status", "position"),
    )

    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(Identity(), primary_key=True)
    project_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("projects.id", ondelete="CASCADE"))
    title: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(120))
    description: Mapped[str | None] = mapped_column(String(2000))
    status: Mapped[TaskStatus] = mapped_column(
        string_enum(TaskStatus, "status"),
        default=TaskStatus.TODO,
        server_default=TaskStatus.TODO.value,
    )
    priority: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(SmallInteger, default=MEDIUM, server_default=str(MEDIUM))
    due_on: Mapped[date | None]
    assignee_id: Mapped[int | None] = mapped_column(
        ForeignKey("users.id", ondelete="SET NULL"), index=True
    )
    position: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(default=0, server_default="0")
    version: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(server_default="1")
    completed_at: Mapped[datetime | None]

    # Every UPDATE adds 1 to version and checks the old value in its WHERE clause, so two
    # requests that both read version 3 cannot both write: the second gets StaleDataError.
    __mapper_args__ = {"version_id_col": version}
examples.explanation: `Identity()` makes `id` a PostgreSQL identity column, the modern form of `SERIAL`. The `CheckConstraint` repeats the schema's 1 to 3 rule in the database, because Pydantic only guards the API, and scripts, migrations, and other services write rows too. `ondelete="CASCADE"` and `"SET NULL"` let PostgreSQL clean up when a project or a user is deleted. The index matches the board's main query: a project's tasks by status, in position order. `version_id_col` gives optimistic locking: an update that lost a race fails with `StaleDataError` instead of silently overwriting someone else's change.

examples.title: Relationships
examples.prompt: Below the columns, `Task` declares how it links to other models.
examples.code:
project: Mapped[Project] = relationship(back_populates="tasks")
assignee: Mapped[User | None] = relationship()
comments: Mapped[list[Comment]] = relationship(back_populates="task", passive_deletes=True)
tags: Mapped[list[Tag]] = relationship(
    secondary="task_tags", order_by="Tag.name", passive_deletes=True
)
watchers: Mapped[list[TaskWatcher]] = relationship(back_populates="task", passive_deletes=True)
examples.explanation: A relationship is an attribute that loads related rows, like `task.project` or `task.comments`. `Mapped[list[Comment]]` makes it a list, and `Mapped[User | None]` one object or `None`. `back_populates` keeps both sides in step in memory. `secondary="task_tags"` reads a many-to-many link through its join table. `passive_deletes=True` leaves deleting comments to the database's `ON DELETE CASCADE`, instead of loading every comment just to delete it. Relationships load lazily by default, on first access, which is where N+1 queries come from.

examples.title: One base for every model
examples.prompt: `app/db/base.py`, the declarative base and its naming convention.
examples.explanation: Without a naming convention, a constraint you don't name gets a name PostgreSQL makes up, and a migration that has to drop it later must look the name up first. With one, the priority check is always `ck_tasks_priority_range`. `type_annotation_map` says what each Python type becomes. Every `Mapped[datetime]` is a `timestamptz`, so times are stored with their zone, and nobody stores a naive local time by accident.

steps.title: Queries without surprises
steps.body:
SQLAlchemy 2 builds queries with `select()`, and the session runs them:

- `session.scalars(select(Task).where(...))` returns model objects.
- `session.scalar(...)` returns one value, or `None`.
- `session.get(Task, 7)` loads by primary key, and returns the copy the session already holds if there is one.
- `session.execute(...)` returns rows with several columns.

The trap is the N+1 query. Load 20 tasks, then read `task.assignee` on each, and the lazy relationship sends one more SELECT per task: 21 queries for one list. It looks fine with three rows in development and gets slow in production. The fix is to say what you need up front, with a loader option. `joinedload` adds a JOIN to the same query, which suits a single related object. `selectinload` sends one more `SELECT ... WHERE ... IN (...)` for all the rows at once, which suits lists. Then guard it with a test that counts statements.

examples.title: Filters and pages
examples.prompt: `list_tasks` in `app/repositories/tasks.py` builds one statement from the filters, then counts it and pages it.
examples.explanation: The statement grows one `.where()` per filter, so filters combine with AND, and every value travels as a bound parameter, never pasted into the SQL. `escape_like` makes `%` and `_` in a search literal, so searching for `80%` finds "80%". The count runs on the filtered statement before `limit` and `offset`, so `total` counts every match, not just this page. `_ordering` sorts by the chosen column and then by id, so rows with equal keys keep the same order from one page to the next.

examples.title: The board in three statements
examples.prompt: `board` in `app/repositories/tasks.py` loads a project's tasks with their assignees and tags, and the comment counts.
examples.code:
def board(session: Session, project_id: int) -> tuple[list[Task], dict[int, int]]:
    """A project's tasks in board order, with assignees and tags loaded, and comment counts.

    Three statements whatever the number of tasks: the tasks joined to their assignees, one
    SELECT ... IN for all their tags, and one grouped count of comments.
    """
    statement = (
        select(Task)
        .where(Task.project_id == project_id)
        .options(joinedload(Task.assignee), selectinload(Task.tags))
        .order_by(Task.status, Task.position, Task.id)
    )
    tasks = list(session.scalars(statement))
    counts = (
        select(Comment.task_id, func.count())
        .join(Task, Task.id == Comment.task_id)
        .where(Task.project_id == project_id)
        .group_by(Comment.task_id)
    )
    return tasks, dict(session.execute(counts).all())
examples.explanation: `joinedload(Task.assignee)` fetches each task's assignee in the same query, through a JOIN. `selectinload(Task.tags)` fetches the tags of every task in one more query. The comment counts come from one `GROUP BY`, instead of loading every comment to count it in Python. So the board costs three statements for 5 tasks or for 60.

examples.title: Proving it with tests
examples.prompt: Every list endpoint has a test that compares statement counts for a small and a big data set. `-k` runs every test whose name contains a word.

examples.explanation: Each test builds two data sets, counts the SQL statements one request runs for each, and asserts the counts are equal. Comparing two sizes is the point: the token and permission checks add a fixed number of queries, and only a query per row makes the counts differ. The day someone reads a lazy relationship in a loop, one of these fails. The output starts where pytest begins collecting, after its header.

steps.title: Migrations with Alembic
steps.body:
`Base.metadata.create_all()` can create tables, but it never changes a table that exists. So a real project changes its schema through migrations. Alembic keeps them in `migrations/versions/`, one file per change, each with an `upgrade()` and a `downgrade()`, chained by `down_revision`. The `alembic_version` table records which one the database is at.

The day-to-day loop:

1. Change a model.
2. Run `uv run alembic revision --autogenerate -m "add task position"`, which compares the models with the database and writes a draft.
3. Read the draft. Autogenerate can't see a rename, so it writes a drop and an add, which loses data, and it never fills in rows.
4. Run `uv run alembic upgrade head`, and commit the file with the model change.

Taskboard's `env.py` takes the database URL from the app's settings, never from `alembic.ini`, so the app and its migrations always point at the same database.

examples.title: A migration that backfills
examples.prompt: `migrations/versions/0002_task_position.py` adds a required column to a table that already has rows.
examples.code:
def upgrade() -> None:
    op.add_column("tasks", sa.Column("position", sa.Integer(), nullable=True))
    op.execute(
        """
        UPDATE tasks
        SET position = numbered.row_number - 1
        FROM (
            SELECT id, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY project_id, status ORDER BY id)
            FROM tasks
        ) AS numbered
        WHERE tasks.id = numbered.id
        """
    )
    op.alter_column("tasks", "position", nullable=False, server_default="0")
    op.create_index(
        "ix_tasks_project_id_status_position", "tasks", ["project_id", "status", "position"]
    )
    op.drop_index("ix_tasks_project_id_status", table_name="tasks")


def downgrade() -> None:
    op.create_index("ix_tasks_project_id_status", "tasks", ["project_id", "status"])
    op.drop_index("ix_tasks_project_id_status_position", table_name="tasks")
    op.drop_column("tasks", "position")
examples.explanation: A new `NOT NULL` column can't be added to a table with rows in one step, because the existing rows have no value for it. So it takes three: add it as nullable, fill it, then set `NOT NULL`. The backfill numbers each column's tasks 0, 1, 2 in id order with a window function, in one UPDATE, instead of a loop in Python. It's written in SQL, not with the app's `Task` model, because the model keeps changing and an old migration must still run years later. `downgrade()` undoes each step in reverse order.

examples.title: Where Alembic connects
examples.prompt: `migrations/env.py` points Alembic at the app's models and settings.
examples.code:
import app.models  # noqa: F401  (every model, so the metadata knows every table)
from app.core.config import get_settings
from app.db.base import Base

config = context.config
if config.config_file_name is not None:
    fileConfig(config.config_file_name)

target_metadata = Base.metadata


def run_migrations_online() -> None:
    if (connection := config.attributes.get("connection")) is not None:
        context.configure(connection=connection, target_metadata=target_metadata)
        with context.begin_transaction():
            context.run_migrations()
        return

    engine = create_engine(get_settings().database_url, poolclass=pool.NullPool)
    with engine.connect() as connection:
        context.configure(connection=connection, target_metadata=target_metadata)
        with context.begin_transaction():
            context.run_migrations()
examples.explanation: `import app.models` loads every model, so `Base.metadata` knows every table when autogenerate compares. The URL comes from `get_settings()`, the same settings the app reads, so `DATABASE_URL` decides for both. A caller may pass an open connection in `config.attributes`, which is how the tests migrate the test database. `NullPool` fits a short script that needs one connection and no pool. Alembic 1.20 reads its settings from `[tool.alembic]` in `pyproject.toml`, and `alembic.ini` only configures its logging.

examples.prompt: Run every migration on an empty database, ask where it stands, then check that the models agree with it.

examples.explanation: Each `Running upgrade` line is one file, applied in chain order from 0001 to 0006, with its docstring as the message. `current` reads the `alembic_version` table, and `0006 (head)` means the database is up to date. `check` compares the models with the migrated database: "No new upgrade operations detected" means no model change is missing its migration. Run it in CI, so a model change can't ship without one. In the workspace the database is already at head, so `upgrade head` prints only the first two lines.

recap:
- Type columns with `Mapped[...]`: `X | None` decides `NULL`, and `mapped_column()` adds lengths, keys, defaults, and indexes.
- Put rules in the database too, with CHECK, UNIQUE, and foreign keys, and give constraints stable names with a naming convention.
- Build queries with `select()`, load relationships up front with `joinedload` or `selectinload`, and test statement counts to stop N+1 queries.
- Change the schema only through Alembic: autogenerate a draft, read it, and add a required column in three steps.
- Run `alembic check` in CI so a model change can't ship without its migration.
